rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that they will be questioned is a chastening, disgraceful sarcasm used in moments of severe anger; the Qur’an uses this style elsewhere.
rows.anchor: here are to chasten and disgrace them. At occasions of severe anger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their affluence was a divine favour testing gratitude, but they claimed it as inheritance, merit, and entitlement, then rebelled against its giver; the mentioned dwellings are their palaces.
rows.anchor: these people were blessed with affluence as a favour from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only after the torment arrived did they recognize their own wrongdoing: the Messenger had fully warned them, but they ignored him and had even demanded the torment.
rows.anchor: they had afflicted injustice on their own self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word daʿwā means raising an outcry and pleading; their continued wailing could not help once the torment had arrived.
rows.anchor: Here it refers to the same wailing which is mentioned in the previous verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people are likened to cut grass whose dry heaps are burned into ashes, becoming dust; the grammatical form agrees with the metaphor’s referent, a common Arabic style.
rows.anchor: just as after grass being cut, its dry mounds are set on fire and it becomes a heap of ashes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage argues that accountability follows from creation as an expression of divine mercy and justice: the obedient are rewarded and those who spread disorder are punished.
rows.anchor: A day of accountability will come in which

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without a final account, the Creator would seem unconcerned with good, evil, justice, or injustice, as though creation were mere entertainment; this contradicts God’s attributes.
rows.anchor: This notion is an obvious farce and totally against the attributes of justice and mercy of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possibility of deities sharing governance and rescuing worshippers would make judgement meaningless, since intercessors could save them regardless of their deeds.
rows.anchor: intercessors and deities exist who share governance with God to the extent that they can save their worshippers from His grasp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe itself testifies that a just, wise, merciful Creator made it for a serious purpose, not amusement, a divine battlefield, or a fairy tale.
rows.anchor: this universe by its very existence testifies that it has been made by a just and wise, merciful and gracious creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every entity points to a great purpose, whose fulfilment and manifestation on a day of judgement follows necessarily from God’s justice and wisdom.
rows.anchor: The obvious consequence of His justice and wisdom is that a day come when this objective will manifest itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating the world as amusement is incompatible with God’s majesty; if He wanted amusement, He could have created it around Himself without involving creatures.
rows.anchor: had this been His plan, He could have made something around Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If no judgement followed the suffering of the oppressed and the trials of diverse people, God’s world would resemble a Roman emperor’s cruel theatre; the Creator’s relation to creatures requires judgement.
rows.anchor: it would only mean that this world too is a theatre of Roman emperors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgement is where truth prevails and evil is eliminated; without it, the world becomes amusement contrary to God’s attributes.
rows.anchor: The relationship of God with His creatures necessitates the advent of a Judgement day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God had no need to make a world of conflict between truth and falsehood, justice and injustice, and oppressor and oppressed merely as a spectacle.
rows.anchor: There was no need for Him to create a place in which there was an eternal conflict between Adam’s progeny and Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It would violate divine justice and mercy to watch creatures suffer through this struggle without rewarding those who serve good and punishing those who support evil.
rows.anchor: It is against God’s justice and mercy that He create such a place of conflict for His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing phrase rules out the idea that God made creation for play; rejecting the hereafter tacitly makes the world mere recreation.
rows.anchor: rejecting the hereafter in fact means that this world is a place of recreation

rows.speaker: polytheistic nations
rows.claim: They pictured the universe as a conflict among gods and goddesses, while Hindu philosophers called it a fairy tale of their supreme God.
rows.anchor: polytheistic nations of this world regarded this universe to be a place of conflict between gods and goddesses

rows.speaker: atheists and non-believers
rows.claim: Though they do not say it openly, rejecting the hereafter leaves the same notion in their minds: the world is recreation rather than a place of truth and justice.
rows.anchor: this evil concept is lodged in their minds too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yadmigh means to strike and injure someone so that the brain is opened.
rows.anchor: The verb يدمغ means to strike and injure someone in a way that it opens up the brain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The respite given to evil alongside truth does not mean equality; it tests which people choose truth and which cling to evil.
rows.anchor: it is not because both are equal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth will strike evil decisively and destroy it at once, like a blow to the brain that immediately kills.
rows.anchor: just as a decisive blow on the brain gives immediate death to a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned words include their claims that the world is sport and that polytheistic intercession can protect them; these beliefs bring ruin.
rows.anchor: refer to their view that this world is a place of sport and recreation

rows.speaker: idolaters
rows.claim: They expected their deities and intercessors to rescue them from danger in the hereafter, so they felt no fear of it.
rows.anchor: they reckoned that if ever the hereafter comes, their deities and intercessors will save them from every danger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the argument for judgement from God’s attributes, the text turns to monotheism: all that is in heaven and earth belongs to God as creatures and servants, without authority.
rows.anchor: All that is in the heavens and the earth are His creatures and servants and have no position of authority with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those in God’s presence are His favoured angels, who remain tireless in worship; this refutes worshippers who regarded them as divine daughters with influence over God.
rows.anchor: refer to the favoured angels of God

rows.speaker: idolaters
rows.claim: They worshipped angels as God’s daughters, believed the angels could secure their wishes and attributed worldly favours and hoped-for afterlife rank to them.
rows.anchor: They reckoned that these angels had a high status before God and also had their way with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels on whose status people rely never stop worshipping, tire, or cease glorifying God.
rows.anchor: they themselves neither cease from worshipping Him nor ever feel worn-out in this act

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression about God reviving the earth means making it lush and green after dryness; 43:11 provides a parallel.
rows.anchor: God revived the earth and made it lush and green after it had become dry and desolate

rows.speaker: polytheists
rows.claim: Some held that the heavens belonged to the throne-God while earthly deities separately governed the earth, which they worshipped instead.
rows.anchor: Many of them thought that the heavens and the earth had separate deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coordination between heaven and earth, including rain reviving dry land, shows one governing mind; separate deities would have caused both realms to collapse.
rows.anchor: This harmony shows that it is governed by a single mind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God master of the throne means His directive prevails in both heaven and earth, leaving no room for others to interfere.
rows.anchor: When He is the master of the throne, then it is His directive which prevails both in the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is not answerable to anyone, while every other being, including angels and humans, is answerable to Him and will be taken to task for disobedience.
rows.anchor: He is not accountable to anyone; all else whether they are angels or human beings are accountable to Him

rows.speaker: idolaters
rows.claim: They imagined their deities shared in governing the universe, could influence God’s decisions, and could act independently without being questioned.
rows.anchor: They thought that they had enough influence on God to make Him change His decision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appeal to historical revelation is a distinct proof for monotheism from the earlier proof based on nature’s harmony; claimants to other gods bear the burden of proof.
rows.anchor: These verses present historical evidence in favour of monotheism and refutation of polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an and earlier prophets all teach monotheism, while opponents reject it from ignorance rather than evidence; this also reassures the Prophet and his followers.
rows.anchor: it is not that these people have any proof on the basis of which they are opposing monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An incomplete verb is understood before the phrase about monotheism, which explains the teaching shared by the Prophet’s community and earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: An incomplete verb is suppressed before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although earlier scriptures contain interpolations, their monotheistic teaching remains; later polytheism arose from followers’ philosophies, just as Qur’an followers also adopted polytheistic practices against its clear teaching.
rows.anchor: the teaching of monotheism is even today preserved in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah, Gospel, Psalms, and Torah’s account of Abraham support the claim that all prophets taught monotheism, never polytheism.
rows.anchor: all available record of previous scriptures corroborates the claim

rows.speaker: idolaters
rows.claim: They called angels God’s daughters and expected worldly favours and high rank in the afterlife through their intercession, a belief that would make judgement meaningless.
rows.anchor: They regard angels to be daughters of God and foolishly think that whatever favours and sustenance they receive in this world is because of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is far beyond having a wife or children; angels are honoured servants, not daughters, and their rank comes from devotion rather than influence over God.
rows.anchor: angels are not daughters of God as these foolish people contend; they are His honourable servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels cannot initiate speech or wield influence; they speak only when permitted and obey God, so hoping they will secure any desired rank is foolish.
rows.anchor: angels cannot even take the initiative in speaking to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels speak only with permission, answer respectfully, and cannot independently secure people from God’s judgement or grant them a rank.
rows.anchor: They only speak when they are permitted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the angels’ past, present, and future; they cannot recommend anyone on their own, intercede only for those God chooses, and tremble in awe, so their intercession cannot oppose truth.
rows.anchor: They can only recommend those whom God chooses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those relying on angelic intercession should reconsider rather than ruin their future on a baseless hope.
rows.anchor: people who have pinned their hopes on their intercession should contemplate all these things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though idolaters treat their deities as if God were their pawn, their true fate is Hell, as for all polytheists; the same warning is given to Christians about Jesus and his mother.
rows.anchor: their real status is spelled out by this verse. Their fate is Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah turns from arguments based on human nature, intellect, and God’s attributes to signs in the world, answering earlier demands for signs; existing signs of providence, power, mercy, monotheism, and the hereafter should suffice.
rows.anchor: this universe is replete with signs of God’s providence, power and mercy and of the belief of monotheism and the advent of the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who have ignored the many existing signs have no guarantee that another new sign would make them see.
rows.anchor: what guarantee is there that that a new sign will open their eyes

none: Bare sūrah title and heading only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s invitation to his father and people is linked to the fate of those who relied on supposed deities and intercessors and ignored the hereafter; the repeated refrain closes the account.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s (sws) invitation to his father and to his nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s people arrogantly reject his invitation and are drowned, followed by the repeated refrain.
rows.anchor: They arrogantly denied it and thereafter were drowned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud’s people, ʿĀd, haughtily reject him and are struck by God’s scourge; the refrain recurs at the end.
rows.anchor: His nation haughtily rejected him. As a result, they were visited by God’s scourge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Salih’s invitation to Thamud ends with their rejection, fate, and the repeated refrain.
rows.anchor: His nation rejected him and met its fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah relates Lot’s invitation, his people’s response, and their fate, then repeats the refrain.
rows.anchor: The invitation of Lot (sws) to his nation is mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shuʿayb account concerns how Madyan treated him and his invitation, ending with their fate and the recurring refrain.
rows.anchor: The way the people of Madyan treated Shu‘ayb (sws) and his invitation is referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion explains the introduction and says the Qur’an comes by divine revelation through the trustworthy spirit.
rows.anchor: God has revealed it to the Prophet (sws) through the trustworthy spirit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation of the Qur’an in Arabic is a great favour to Arabs; failure to value it is their deprivation and misfortune.
rows.anchor: It is God’s great favour to the Arabs that He has revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Previous prophets’ scriptures contain arguments for the Qur’an, known to scholars among the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: Arguments in favour of this Book are found in the scriptures of the previous prophets also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book warns and admonishes disbelievers before accountability so they understand the consequences of persistent denial.
rows.anchor: The Book warns and admonishes the disbelievers in order to fully inform them before calling them to account

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Qur’an inspired by jinn or devils is foolish; the text describes the traits of those who receive satanic inspiration.
rows.anchor: It is extreme foolishness to regard this Book to be inspired by the jinn or the devils

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is God’s work, not poetry, and the passage gives criteria distinguishing it from poetry and prophets from poets.
rows.anchor: It is the work of God. Certain parameters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disconnected letters Ṭā Sīn Mīm are, in the author’s view, the predicate of an omitted subject, a construction supplied in the translation.
rows.anchor: of a suppressed inchoative (mubtadā’). This

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear Book is the Qur’an, whose eloquent presentation and varied sound arguments make it proof of its own truth, like the sun needing no proof; the Prophet need not supply an external sign.
rows.anchor: the Book that he is presenting is the greatest proof of its own veracity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse affectionately reassures the Prophet over his grief at people’s refusal to believe.
rows.anchor: This verse sounds further assurance to the Prophet (sws) in a very affectionate way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and the Book are not at fault when people reject faith; the rejecters invent excuses, while his duty is to communicate, which he has fully performed and continues performing.
rows.anchor: his only responsibility is to communicate, which he has carried out in its ultimate way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expected feminine adjective is replaced by a masculine plural form in agreement with the governed noun in their necks, a common Arabic construction.
rows.anchor: This is a common linguistic style of Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could send a sign that forces submission, but values faith reached through intellect and free choice rather than compulsion.
rows.anchor: Only this kind of faith holds value before Him and not what that is professed due to compulsion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sign verse also reassures the Prophet: God’s established practice is to let people choose faith, so he should not be troubled by demands for signs and should leave the matter to God.
rows.anchor: he should not be worried on their demands and leave their matter to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses repeat the point at the close of al-Furqan: divine reminders are meant to teach people the right way, yet repeated warnings make the rejecters hate the remedy and its messenger more.
rows.anchor: the more measures were taken to cure them, the more they hated the doctor and his prescription

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They have kept evading and mocking the Qur’an and Messenger, so the warnings they mocked will now appear before them one by one.
rows.anchor: the only option that remains is that each and every consequence
